Strengths to preserve: the plan is candid about its gaps (wired prototype, rules-based scoring, no patent, no manufacturing quotes), and the problem framing and pricing structure are clear. To improve the written submission, prioritize the following:

1) Replace assumption-driven market sizing with bottom-up numbers. The 'over one billion dollars' TAM (players x assumed price) is weak and contradicts the admission that not every player needs a glove. Lead with the serviceable market: 20-30K programs x $450 kit and $120/yr subscription (roughly $9-13M in kit revenue plus about $2.4-3.6M recurring). Cite sources for program counts and show how you derived them. Add a realistic obtainable share for years 1-3.

2) Quantify demand validation. '14 coaches' and 'several said they would pay' is soft. Report how many would pay, at what price, and whether anyone gave a pre-order, letter of intent, or deposit. Summarize interview findings (frequency of the problem, current workarounds, budget authority, purchase process) and identify who actually buys in rec leagues (league board, parents, coach out of pocket), since this drives pricing and sales cycle.

3) Evidence that the product works. The core claim is that the score reflects real catch technique, yet it is based on rules from two coaches. Describe a validation plan: compare glove scores against expert coach ratings or video review, test-retest reliability, and sample sizes. Include pilot results with specific numbers rather than 'positive but informal,' and state success criteria for the planned 4-5 team pilot (e.g., coach weekly active use, measurable score improvement over a season, willingness to pay).

4) Be explicit about technical risks. Address durability (sweat, impact, kids' rough use), sizing across growing hands, battery life, wireless reliability, whether sensors alter catching feel, sensor accuracy with different balls and gloves, and safety/compliance considerations for youth products, including data privacy for minors (COPPA and similar). Explain how the wired, single-size prototype gets to a sellable product and what it costs.

5) Tighten unit economics. A $38 prototype BOM is not a COGS figure. Estimate fully loaded cost at 100 and 1,000 units (assembly, packaging, shipping, returns, app hosting, support) and show gross margin on the $450 kit (6 gloves, about $228 in parts alone at prototype cost). Clarify whether a kit of 6 gloves matches how a team uses them given rosters of 12-20 and several receivers. Justify why the $120 subscription is worth paying for in year two, and give a churn assumption.

6) Make the financial model transparent. Provide a simple table: units, price, revenue, COGS, operating costs, and cash by quarter, with stated assumptions (number of teams, conversion, subscription retention). Year-one revenue of $18K implies about 40 kits, which is inconsistent with a pilot of 4-5 teams; reconcile this. Show how year three exceeds $300K (how many teams, what channels) and break-even logic, and acknowledge that near break-even in year two likely excludes a salary and manufacturing capital need.

7) Sharpen the funding ask. Break the $25,000 into a line-item budget tied to milestones (20 gloves, pilot logistics, provisional patent, entity formation, testing) and show it is sufficient to reach a defined next milestone. State what follow-on funding or revenue is required afterward and what evidence will unlock it.

8) Strengthen the competitive and defensibility section. Name specific competitors (smart footballs, wearable sensor and video-analysis tools, general coaching apps) and provide a comparison on price, what is measured, and ease of use. Address the substitute of free or cheap video via phones and AI-based video apps, which may be the strongest threat to a hardware solution. Explain why the glove data is meaningfully better than video, and give a clearer plan for defensibility (provisional patent timing, proprietary dataset from pilots, brand and coach community) rather than only noting the gap.

9) Address go-to-market specifics. Explain how you will reach the 20-30K programs: league partnerships, coaching associations, youth football governing bodies, school athletic budgets, camps, and parent-funded purchases. Estimate customer acquisition cost, sales cycle (youth leagues buy seasonally), and whether the 'regional then state by state' approach is realistic for a seasonal product. Consider whether single-glove parent sales dilute focus or are a useful low-friction entry.

10) Mitigate team gaps visibly. The plan notes no manufacturing experience or industry advisor but offers no concrete mitigation. Name target advisors or contract manufacturers to approach, and include time commitments (are the members full-time students, and can they sustain this through graduation?). Define roles in a way that covers testing, regulatory, and operations.

11) Add a risk and timeline section. Include a 12-month Gantt-style milestone list with owners and dates, and the top 5 risks with mitigations (sensor accuracy, manufacturing cost, seasonal sales window, safety/liability, adoption).

12) Polish the writing. Fix typos ('embeded'), cut hedging language ('we believe', 'if even a small fraction'), lead each section with the key claim and number, add a clear one-line value proposition and a product image or screenshot, and keep the executive summary within a page with the crisp ask and milestone upfront. Avoid claims such as 'every kid regardless of budget' unless pricing supports it, and note that a $450 kit may itself be out of reach for many rec leagues, so describe funding paths (league budgets, sponsorships, grants).

Business plan text:

Gridiron Glove
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: GRIDIRON GLOVE
Problem
Youth football is a very large activity in America with millions of kids playing every fall,
and wide receivers are one of the most technique dependent positions on the field. Catching the
ball with the hands instead of the body, hand position, and timing of the finger close are all
things that can be taught but only if somebody is watching and giving feedback. The problem is
that most youth and middle school football programs are run by volunteer coaches who have a
full roster of kids, limited practice time, and often no specific background in receiver play.
High schools and colleges can use video analysis software and have assistant coaches for each
position group, but youth programs mostly can not afford this. As a result bad habits like body
catching and late hand closure are formed early and stick with players for years. Coaches we
talked to (about 14 so far, mostly from rec leagues and two middle schools near our university)
told us this is one of their biggest frustrations, and several said they would pay for a tool
that tells them what to fix.
Solution
Gridiron Glove is a training glove with embeded sensors paired with a mobile application. The
glove has pressure sensors in the palm and fingertips plus a small motion sensor on the back of
the hand. When a player catches a ball the glove records the contact pattern and the timing and
the app converts that into a catch technique score from 0 to 100. The score breaks down into
sub scores such as hand placement, finger closure timing, and whether the ball was secured with
hands only or trapped to the chest. After a practice session the app shows the coach a simple
team dashboard, ranks players, and suggests specific drills from a library tied to each
weakness. The coach does not need to review video or understand biomechanics. Our software is
designed to be simple enough to use on a phone at the field while kids are doing reps.
Our prototype currently works with one glove size and a wired connection to a small battery
pack and our scoring is based on rules we developed with advice from two coaches rather than a
large data set. Wireless and multiple sizes are on the roadmap.
Market
According to widely cited industry figures there are several million youth tackle and flag
football players in the United States and hundreds of thousands of youth teams. If even a small
fraction of these teams bought a set of gloves, this would be a meaningful market. We estimate
the total addressable market at over one billion dollars by multiplying the number of players
by an assumed price, though we realize that not every player needs their own glove. Our more
realistic serviceable market is youth leagues and middle school programs that already spend
money on equipment, which we think is roughly 20 to 30 thousand programs. Our first target is
the region around our university where we have relationships with a number of leagues, and then
expanding state by state.
Business Model
We plan to sell a team kit of 6 gloves with the software included for the first year, priced
around 450 dollars, and then charge an annual software subscription of about 120 dollars per
team after that for the dashboard, drill library and updates. We also plan to sell single
gloves to parents and individual players at roughly 99 dollars, and to sell to private receiver
training camps. Our cost to build each glove at prototype stage is around 38 dollars in parts,
and we believe this could fall at volume but we have not gotten manufacturing quotes yet.
Longer term we see revenue from league wide licensing deals and from data insights, though the
data side is early thinking.
Competition

There are video analysis platforms used by high school and college programs, but these are
expensive and need cameras and staff time. There are also smart ball products and passing
machines that help with throwing and catching drills but they do not measure what the hands are
doing at the moment of the catch. Some general wearable sensor companies serve pro and college
athletes at high price points. We are not aware of a product that targets youth coaches
specifically with a low cost glove and drill suggestions. Our advantage is price, simplicity,
and focus on a single position skill. Of course a bigger company could enter this space, and we
have not filed any patents yet, which is a gap we know about.
Team
Marcus Delaney Otieno is our CEO and leads partnerships, he played receiver in high school and
has coached a youth flag league for two seasons. Priya Raghunathan-Bell is CTO and leads
hardware, she is a senior in electrical engineering with experience from a sensor research lab.
Tobias Wendelstrom leads software and the mobile app and is studying computer science. Dani
Kowalczyk-Reyes handles marketing and finance and is a business major who built our website. We
do not yet have a team member with manufacturing experience or a formal advisor from the sports
equipment industry, and we are looking to add one.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype glove and a basic version of
the app, registered the company, and launched a website. We have tested the prototype with a
small number of players at two practices and collected early feedback which was positive though
the sample is small and informal. We have spent roughly 2,300 dollars to date, funded by team
members and a small university grant. Our next 12 months plan is to build 20 improved gloves,
run a pilot with 4 to 5 youth teams, get manufacturing quotes, and file a provisional patent.
We project revenue of about 18 thousand dollars in year one from pilot sales, growing to over
300 thousand dollars by year three, though these projections are based on assumptions about
adoption that we still need to validate. We expect to be near break even at the end of year two
if we keep the team lean.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to the competition for funding, mentorship and visibility. We are requesting
25,000 dollars in prize or seed funding which we would use for improved prototype production,
pilot costs, legal fees for the patent and for forming our legal entity, and basic testing.
Just as important, we would like to be connected to mentors with experience in consumer
hardware manufacturing, youth sports organizations, and early stage fundraising. We believe
Gridiron Glove can make quality receiver coaching available to every kid regardless of their
team's budget and we would be grateful for the chance to compete.
Question: What can the team do to improve their written submission?
